slides.title: Introduction to Data Collection
slides.text:
Introduction to Data Collection
Data collection is the systematic process of gathering information for research or analysis.
Choosing appropriate sources and methods ensures the reliability and relevance of results.

bullets.text: Data collection is the systematic process of gathering information for research or analysis.
Choosing appropriate sources and methods ensures the reliability and relevance of results.

slides.title: Primary Data
slides.text:
Primary Data
First-hand data collected by the investigator specifically for a purpose.
Examples: observations, surveys, lab experiments, interviews, physical tests.

bullets.text: First-hand data collected by the investigator specifically for a purpose.
Examples: observations, surveys, lab experiments, interviews, physical tests.

slides.title: Characteristics of Primary Data
slides.text:
Characteristics of Primary Data
Original, specific to the research question, often more accurate and up-to-date.
Involves higher cost and time investment; researcher controls the collection process

bullets.text: Original, specific to the research question, often more accurate and up-to-date.
Involves higher cost and time investment; researcher controls the collection process

slides.title: Secondary Data
slides.text:
Secondary Data
Information already collected and available through other sources.
Examples: government reports, academic articles, books, databases, institutional records.

bullets.text: Information already collected and available through other sources.
Examples: government reports, academic articles, books, databases, institutional records.

slides.title: Characteristics of Secondary Data
slides.text:
Characteristics of Secondary Data
Already exists, typically less expensive and quicker to access.
May lack specificity/accuracy for current research, possible bias or outdatedness.

bullets.text: Already exists, typically less expensive and quicker to access.
May lack specificity/accuracy for current research, possible bias or outdatedness.

slides.title: Primary vs. Secondary Data
slides.text:
Primary vs. Secondary Data
Feature | Primary Data | Secondary Data
Definition | Collected first-hand | Pre-existing data
Sources | Surveys, experiments, interviews | Reports, articles, records
Advantages | Accurate, relevant | Cost-effective, accessible
Drawbacks | Costly, time-consuming | Possible lack of fit, bias

Observational: Directly recording behaviors or phenomena.
Survey-based: Questionnaires, online forms for self-reported data.
Experimental: Manipulating variables to observe effects.

slides.title: Designing a Data Collection Plan
slides.text:
Designing a Data Collection Plan
Step 1: Choose a research question (e.g., study habits, food choices).
Step 2: Decide on primary, secondary, or mixed approach.
Step 3: Draft data collection procedure (survey/experiment outline).
Step 4: Identify sources and plan data recording/storage.

slides.title: Evaluation of Information Sources
slides.text:
Evaluation of Information Sources
Factors on which an information source is evaluated:
Purpose: Why does the source exist? To identify the type and bias of information presented
Authority: What are the credentials of the authors/organisation sponsoring the source?
Scope: How much information is available? Selective or Comprehensive? How old is the data?
Audience: Whom does the source cater to? Level of knowledge assumed from the audience?
Format: How quickly can you find the information? How easy is it to access the source?

slides.title: Terms in Research
slides.text:
Terms in Research
Concept: generally accepted collection of meanings or characteristics associated with certain events, objects, conditions, situations and behaviour. E.g.: “leadership”, “productivity”, and “morale”; “gross national product”, “asset”, and “inflation”.
Construct: an abstract idea invented for research or theory-building purposes. Build out of simpler and concrete concepts, especially when the intended idea is not subject to direct observation. E.g.: Hypothetical Constructs.
Definition: a statement explaining the meaning of a concept.
There are two types of definition: dictionary definition and operational definition (defined in terms of specific criteria for testing or measurement.
Variable: a symbol of an event, act, characteristic, trait or attribute (parts of the construct) that can be measured or assigned categorical values.
Types of Variables: Independent, Dependent, Extraneous, Control, Moderating, Compounding and Intervening.

slides.title: Terms in Research
slides.text:
Terms in Research
Propositions: a statement about observable phenomena (concepts) that may be considered true or false.
Hypothesis: a proposition is formulated for empirical testing.
Types of Hypotheses: Descriptive, Relational, Correlational, and Causal
Descriptive: state the existence of some variable
Relational: state a relationship between two variables for a case
Correlational: state that variables occur together in some specified manner without implying causal direction.
Causal: it also implies the existence of a cause-and-effect relationship between variables
Theory: a supposition or a system of validated hypotheses intended to explain phenomena. Theory has two purposes: predicting and understanding a phenomenon.
Theory differs from hypothesis in terms of complexity and abstraction. Theories are more complex and abstract and tend to have more variables than hypotheses.
Model: a representation of a system that is constructed to study.
Models differ from theories as theories are intended to explain, and models are intended to represent.

slides.title: Descriptive Hypotheses
slides.text:
Descriptive Hypotheses
Descriptive hypotheses state the existence, size, form, or distribution of some variable
Descriptive
In Detroit, our potato chip market share stands at 13.7%.
American cities are experiencing budget difficulties.
Eighty percent of Company Z stockholders (cases) favor increasing the company’s cash dividend (variable).
Research Question
What is the market share for our potato chips in Detroit?
Are American cities experiencing budget difficulties?
Do stockholders of Company Z favor an increased cash dividend?

slides.title: Relational Hypotheses
slides.text:
Relational Hypotheses
Relational Hypotheses are statements that describe a relationship between two variables with respect to some case
Example: Foreign (variable) cars are perceived by American consumers (case) to be of better quality (variable) than domestic cars.
In this instance, the nature of the relationship between the two variables (“country of origin” and “perceived quality”) is not specified
Is there only an implication that the variables occur in some predictable relationship, or is one variable somehow responsible for the other?

slides.title: Hypotheses
slides.text:
Hypotheses
A hypothesis serves several important functions:
It guides the direction of the study.
It identifies facts that are relevant and those that are not.
It suggests which form of research design is likely to be most appropriate.
It provides a framework for organizing the conclusions that result.
Example: Husbands and wives agree in their perceptions of their respective roles in purchase decisions.
The hypothesis specifies who shall be studied (married couples), in what context they shall be studied (their consumer decision making), and what shall be studied (their individual perceptions of their roles)

slides.title: Terms in Research
slides.text:
Terms in Research
Exposition: a statement that describes without attempting an explanation.
Argument: a statement allows us to explain, interpret, defend, challenge, and explore meaning.
Deduction: a conclusive argument – i.e. a conclusion must necessarily follow from the results given.
Induction: an inferred argument – i.e. a conclusion from one or more particular facts or pieces of evidence.

slides.title: Types of Research
slides.text:
Types of Research
Exploratory vs Descriptive vs Analytical (or Explanatory)
Exploratory: research to gain familiarity
Descriptive: description of the existing state of affairs at present
Analytical or Explanatory: uses available information and analyses it to make a critical evaluation of causation
Fundamental (Basic) vs Applied (or Action)
Fundamental: for a generalised area to build on the literature/existing theory
Applied: for a specific application
Quantitative vs Qualitative
Quantitative: based on measurement of quantity or amount. An objective assessment of data using quantitative methods.
Qualitative: based on quality or kind. A subjective assessment of emotions, opinions and behaviours.
Conceptual (Theoretical) vs Empirical (Experimental) vs Simulation
Conceptual: Based on some abstract area or theory
Empirical: based on experience or observation (Often without due regard to theory)
Simulation: based on observations made in an artificial environment

slides.title: Types of Variables
slides.text:
Types of Variables
Dependent and Independent Variables: If one variable depends upon or is a consequence of the other variable, it is termed a dependent variable, and the variable that is antecedent to the dependent variable is termed an independent variable.
Extraneous Variables: Independent variables that are not considered for the study’s purpose but may affect the dependent variable are extraneous variables.
Control Variables: The control variable is used to minimise the effects of extraneous variables. They are measured, but their effect is not hypothesised.
Moderator Variables: Moderator variables are variables like control variables, but instead of having an effect on other variables, they impact the relationship between variables. Moderator variables are also measured, and their effect is hypothesised.
For simplicity's sake, consider moderating variables as catalysts that make a relationship between independent and dependent variables stronger or weaker. Control variables are variables that you are not particularly interested in, but they can have a material effect on your dependent variable, and you wish to eliminate their effects from the effect of your independent variable of interest on your dependent variable.
Mediator Variables: A mediating variable (or mediator) explains how two variables are related

slides.title: Data Cleaning and Preparation
slides.text:
Data Cleaning and Preparation
Data quality dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity
Impact on analysis: biased results, reduced power, faulty decisions
Clean data eliminates inaccuracies, missing values, and duplicates that could bias results.
It ensures consistency across data sources, facilitating comparison and integration.
Clean data reduces computational effort and speeds up analysis.
It increases the reliability and validity of models, predictions, and insights.
